title: What is known about 1RB1LC_1LA1RE_0RD0LA_---1LB_1LD0RF_0RE1RB
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LC_1LA1RE_0RD0LA_---1LB_1LD0RF_0RE1RB.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.

Its run is a binary counter on the left, whose overflows come at doubling times, and a word of binary digits on the right through which each overflow moves a marker one block; when the marker reaches the end of the tape the word is rebuilt longer and the counter starts again.
verdict: The question is open. Lean proves no halt in the first 1.2·1070 steps: a certificate written by the accelerated simulator is accepted by a checker whose soundness is checked by Lean's kernel (the check itself is one native_decide evaluation). The C simulator finds no halt in the first 1011 steps.

What it does. At each overflow of its left counter the tape is C>0 (1 0)^z W. Every shuttle of the head adds one to the z-digit counter L on the left and one to a binary counter R whose bits sit in fixed slots of W; when L overflows (z grows by one) R has gained 2z, and W changes by exactly one binary carry starting at slot z. Late in an epoch that carry moves a marker bit one block right per overflow, with gaps obeying D' = 2D + 2 exactly. When R overflows the word is rebuilt (steps 17,682,600, 5,745,422,543, 49,800,461,566).

Why it is hard. The counter laws are checked by Lean only for the digit layouts the run actually meets, not for all words, and the rebuilds are not understood. A halt needs F to read two 0s in a row, which on the right sweep means reaching the end of the tape in F: Lean proves a sweep entering the last block in E does that exactly when the block has length 1 mod 3. In 1.6·1045 steps the end is reached 83 times, never in F; why the rebuilt words keep it so is not proved.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (D0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: A sound checker for long runs
claims.text: A certificate is a list of plain runs and batches of counter ticks. For a batch the checker cuts the tape into the two counters by a given layout (and confirms the cut by rebuilding the tape), runs the left and right parts of one tick on windows holding only the low digits, for every carry length, and requires each to end with its digits incremented. Proved for any certificate: if the checker accepts it with step count N, the machine runs N steps from blank tape. The window runs fail rather than look outside their window, so their results hold for any surrounding tape; the step count of d ticks is in closed form.

claims.title: No halt in the first 1.2·10<sup>70</sup> steps
claims.text: The certificate lean/cert.txt (60,256 operations, 20,226 of them batches, written by py/accel.py cert 1e70) is accepted: the machine runs 12,198,487,909,209,082,368,679,859,826,732,096,416,911,140,917,107,868,420,374,132,270,946,987 steps from blank tape without halting, and a halt, if any, comes later. The evaluation is compiled code (about 4 minutes).

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>11</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/tmrun.c runs 1011 steps without a halt; 385 cells visited, 312 ones at the end.

claims.title: The overflow configurations of the run
claims.text: All 144 moments in the first 1011 steps where C is at the left end on 0 1 0 have the shape (1 0)^z W with W of odd blocks; z rises by one from each to the next except at 16 restructures where it falls back to 1 or 2, the last three at steps 17,682,600, 5,745,422,543 and 49,800,461,566.
claims.where: tmrun ... records, read in pairs of cells

claims.title: Random words of the same shape halt
claims.text: Started from C>0 (1 0)^z W with random short words W, the machine often halts within a hundred steps (in state D reading the 0 next to the last cell), so non-halting is a property of the words the run writes, not of the shape.
claims.where: experiments with a direct simulator started from given tapes

claims.title: The overflow law: one binary carry per overflow
claims.text: For consecutive overflow events (z, W) and (z + 1, W') of the run, W' differs from W by one binary carry (digits p<sub>1</sub> < … < p<sub>k</sub>, 1 → 0 at all but the last, 0 → 1 at the last) at 55 of the 106 pairs up to 2·10<sup>9</sup> steps (96 of 162 up to 5·10<sup>10</sup>); the other pairs are restructures and their aftermath. Re-running one event (step 17,857,444) with every z from 0 to 16 shows the carry always starts at a fixed slot for z (slots 2, 5, 8, 11, 18, 21, 24, …, 3 digits apart with a few separators): W holds a binary number R and an overflow at length z adds 2<sup>z</sup>.

claims.title: The marker and the doubling gaps
claims.text: Late in an epoch W = P 111110 (110)^b 111 in digits (the marker is the single 1 bit of R's high part, cells 1^11 0); each overflow gives P 110 111110 (110)^(b-1) 111, and the gap D between overflows becomes exactly 2D + 2: 26 such moves and 23 consecutive pairs, all as predicted, in the first 5·1010 steps.

claims.title: Two counters on one clock
claims.text: Between overflows the head shuttles around a point near the start of W; the turning points left of it follow the ruler sequence of a binary counter (L, digits as cell pairs 0 0/1 1) and those right of it the ruler sequence of a second one (R, the slots of W). The overflow law is what this predicts.
claims.where: turning points of the head between steps 17,857,444 and 18,032,242

claims.title: Restructures are set off by R
claims.text: From the event at step 9,008,202, re-run with z = 5..13, R overflows before L and the next event is a restructure after 3,441,111 to 3,453,981 steps, about the same for every z; what it writes depends on z (the digits of L are copied into the new word).

claims.title: The right sweep and the end of the tape
claims.text: E> (111)^n reaches (011)^n E> on any tape; a last block 1^(3n+1) entered in E ends in D on a 0, where the machine halts, and blocks 1^(3n+2), 1^(3n+3) turn back in A or D on a 1.

claims.title: The accelerated simulator agrees with the direct run
claims.text: py/accel.py learns the digits of the two counters and the step cost of a tick by carry lengths, and applies runs of ticks arithmetically; it gives the 126 overflow events of the first 2·1010 steps with exactly the step counts, z and W of tools/c/tmrun.c.

claims.title: The right end of the tape in 1.6·10<sup>45</sup> steps
claims.text: In the accelerated run to 1.6·1045 steps (842 events, 23 rebuilds, the last at 1.47·1042, W grown to 782 digits) the head reaches blank tape at the right 83 times, in E (24) or B (59), never in F: three times an epoch, ending ...011011011, ...110110101, ...101101101.

claims.title: The restructures, and the question itself
claims.text: Not known: the tick of the two counters for all words (Lean checks it only on the layouts of the run, so the overflow law for all z is not a theorem), the rule of a rebuild as a function of (z, L, W), why the rebuilt words are never entered by the right sweep in a way that reaches the end of the tape in F, and whether the machine halts.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. Started on a blank tape, this Turing machine runs for at least 1.2·10<sup>70</sup> steps without stopping, a bound checked in Lean. Two binary counters tick together; each overflow of the left one adds a power of two to the right one, which shows up as a marker moving through a word, and when the right one overflows the word is rebuilt. This page runs the real machine in your browser and lists what is known.

facts.text: No halt, proved in Lean from a certificate of 20,226 batches of counter ticks.
The word is rebuilt 23 times by 1.6·10<sup>45</sup> steps, the last at 1.5·10<sup>42</sup>.
Each overflow of the left counter adds 2<sup>z</sup> to the number in the word: one binary carry.

sections.heading: A counter and a marker
html:
Stop the simulator whenever the head, in state C, is at the left end of the tape reading a 0 followed by 1 0. From the head on the tape then reads C>0 (1 0)^z W, where W is a word of odd blocks of 1s separated by single 0s. Read in pairs of cells, the tape is a string of binary digits (the second cell of each pair); the prefix is a run of z zero digits.

From one such moment to the next z grows by one and the step count doubles: the prefix is a binary counter, and each of its overflows makes one change to W. In most of the run that change is easy to see. The far end of W is periodic, blocks 1^5 separated by single 0s, with one longer block 1^11, a marker, among them; each overflow moves the marker one block to the right:

stepzend of the tape

(The rows are 2,796,798 and 5,593,598 steps apart.)

sections.heading: Two counters on one clock
html:
Between two overflow events the head does not visit the left end. It shuttles back and forth around a point near the start of W, and each shuttle (a tick) does two things. On its left it adds one to a binary counter L: the z zero digits of the prefix, written while counting in pairs of cells 0 0 and 1 1, lowest digit next to W. On its right it adds one to a second binary counter R whose bits live inside W. You can see both in where the head turns: left of the point the turning places follow the ruler sequence 1, 2, 1, 3, 1, 2, 1, 4, … of L, and right of it the ruler sequence of R.

An overflow event is the moment L has counted all 2z of its values: it is reset, and one digit longer. In those 2z ticks R has gained exactly 2z. That is easy to test: take one event, change only z, and run to the next event. The word changes by one binary carry, and where the carry starts depends only on z:

event at step 17,857,444, W in digits:
    11111011111101101111101111111111100011011111000111111111111110110110…
 z=6 ........................0..0..0..1..................................
 z=7 ...........................0..0..1..................................
 z=9 .................................1..................................
 z=10 ............................................1.......................
 z=12 ..........................................................0..1.......
 z=14 ................................................................1....

So R's bits sit in fixed slots of W, mostly three digits apart (1 1 b), with a few separating stretches, and an overflow at length z adds 2z to R. The bits of R below z never change again in the epoch: they are frozen at whatever the start of the epoch left there.

stepper.note: Starts from the event at step 18,032,242 of the run from blank tape. Eleven applications reach b = 0 at step 733,663,420, as in the run; the marker then merges with the end of the word, and the next restructure of the run came at step 5,745,422,543. The stepper only does the arithmetic of the rule.

sections.heading: Checking 10<sup>70</sup> steps
html:
Lean cannot run 1070 steps one at a time. The accelerated simulator writes a certificate instead: a list of 60,256 operations, either a few thousand plain steps or a batch, which says “both counters go up by d”. A checker in Lean replays it, and a theorem says that whatever the certificate, an accepted one is a real run of the machine.

The checker does not take the simulator's word for a batch. The head has to sit on the base cell, a 0, in state A. Left of it the tape is cut into the digits of L (pairs of equal cells) with the gaps between them; right of it into the digits of R (single cells) with their gaps; the cut is confirmed by putting the tape back together. One tick visits the right side, then the left, then the right again, coming back to the base cell in states A, E and A. For each carry length k the checker runs the left part on a window holding only the lowest k + 1 digits of L, and for each j the right part on a window with the lowest j + 1 digits of R. A window run stops with an error if the head would step outside, so what it shows is true whatever the rest of the tape holds.

proved once, for any machinewhat it gives
wrun_sounda run inside a window is the same run on any tape around it
side_soundthe left and right parts of a tick, checked apart, make the whole tick
tickfrom any counter values: +1 to both, in G(k) + F(j) steps
batchd ticks, in a closed-form step count

The step count of d ticks needs no tick-by-tick sum: among the values a, a + 1, …, a + d − 1 exactly ⌊(a + d + 2k)/2k+1⌋ − ⌊(a + 2k)/2k+1⌋ end in k ones, and each of those ticks costs G(k) on the left. Overflows, new digits and rebuilds fall between batches and are plain steps. The whole check takes about 4 minutes as compiled code (native_decide, which trusts Lean's compiler); the soundness theorems are checked by Lean's kernel.

sections.heading: Restructures
html:
When R overflows, the marker having reached the end of the tape, the word is rebuilt longer and z starts again from 1: a restructure. It is set off by R, not by L: re-running one late event with different z, the restructure comes after the same number of steps for every z large enough, but what it writes depends on z, since the digits of L at that moment are copied into the new word. In the first 1011 steps the last restructures came at steps 17,682,600 (W then has 102 digits), 5,745,422,543 (131 digits) and 49,800,461,566 (163 digits); at step 96,162,430,390 the run is at z = 30 with 192 digits.

The machine halts only in state D reading a 0. Started from configurations of the same shape with random words, it often halts within a hundred steps with D>0 1 at the right end of the tape. The run never meets such words: what it writes at a restructure is special, and what makes it safe has not been worked out. A halt, if there is one, would come out of a restructure.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.063). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).
After 109 steps the tape spans 252 cells (199 left of the start, 50 right), with a density of 1s of 0.802.

The tape (run-length coded, 1^5 is five 1s, C>0 the head in state C on a 0) at some of the last moments the head reached a new cell, cut to 400 characters:

family: binary counter moving a marker through a word
summary: Two binary counters fed by one clock: L (the z zero digits at the left) and R (bits in fixed slots of the word W); each overflow of L adds 2^z to R, and when R overflows the word is rebuilt. A halt needs the right sweep to reach the end of the tape in F (Lean: last block of length 1 mod 3). Open; Lean (certificate checker, native_decide): no halt in 1.2·10^70 steps; the end never reached in F in the run to 1.6·10^45.
